test.title: Key Stage 2 Science - Progress Test 1
sourceInstructions: You have 45 minutes for this test.
The pencil symbol shows where an answer is required.
Some questions in the paper version require a drawn answer.
Do not write in the grey margins or on or near the bar codes.
digitalInstructions: You have 45 minutes for the complete test.
Choose, order, match, classify, or enter an answer as directed.
Every question has been adapted so it can be checked automatically.
Answers and feedback are intended to be shown only after submission.

attribution.adaptationNote: Response formats were adapted for deterministic digital marking; the assessed science and official mark allocation are preserved.

sections.title: Pond life
sections.introduction: Tom holds a glass bowl in pond water and watches the pond life underneath. He sees a water beetle, pondweed and a stickleback fish, and is told that micro-organisms live in the pond water.

questions.originalPrompt: What property of the bowl allows Tom to see the pond life? The glass bowl is ...
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which property of the glass bowl allows Tom to see the pond life through it?

options.label: Transparent (clear or see-through)
options.feedback: Correct: transparent materials let light pass through, so Tom can see through the bowl.

options.label: Opaque
options.feedback: Opaque materials block light, so Tom would not be able to see through the bowl.

options.label: Absorbent
options.feedback: Absorbency describes taking in liquid; it does not explain why Tom can see through the bowl.

options.label: Flexible
options.feedback: Flexibility describes bending; it does not explain why Tom can see through the bowl.

feedback.correct: Correct - the glass is transparent.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the property that lets light pass through a material.
feedback.explanation: A transparent or clear material can be seen through.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from free text to a single-choice property question.

questions.originalPrompt: The stickleback fish is a predator. Tick ONE box to show why the stickleback fish is a predator.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why is the stickleback fish a predator?

options.label: It eats plants.
options.feedback: Eating plants does not make an animal a predator.

options.label: It eats other animals.
options.feedback: Correct: predators hunt or eat other animals.

options.label: It hides near pondweed.
options.feedback: Where it hides does not determine whether it is a predator.

options.label: It gets eaten by other animals.
options.feedback: Being eaten makes it prey in that relationship, not a predator.

feedback.correct: Correct - predators eat other animals.
feedback.incorrect: A predator is identified by what it eats, not where it lives or what eats it.
feedback.explanation: The stickleback is a predator because it eats other animals.

questions.adaptationNote: Original objective format preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: Write true or false next to each statement about producers.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Classify each statement about producers as true or false.

items.statement: Producers are at the start of the food chain.
Producers catch their food from the water.
Producers use sunlight to make new materials for growth.

feedback.correct: Correct - all three statements are classified accurately.
feedback.incorrect: Remember that producers make new material using light; they do not catch food from the water.
feedback.explanation: Producers begin food chains and use sunlight to make material for growth.

questions.adaptationNote: Original true/false format preserved as a digital grid; all three rows are required for the mark.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why Tom cannot see the micro-organisms in the water.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why can Tom not see the micro-organisms in the pond water with his eyes alone?

options.label: They are microscopic - too small to see without a microscope.
options.feedback: Correct: micro-organisms are too small to see with the unaided eye.

options.label: They are transparent, so light always passes through them.
options.feedback: Transparency is not the reason given by the evidence; their extremely small size is.

options.label: They are all hidden behind the pondweed.
options.feedback: They remain too small to see even when they are not behind pondweed.

options.label: They are exactly the same colour as the water.
options.feedback: Colour does not explain why micro-organisms require a microscope to be seen.

feedback.correct: Correct - they are microscopic.
feedback.incorrect: Choose the explanation about their size and the need for a microscope.
feedback.explanation: Micro-organisms are at the very small end of the size scale and are too small for the unaided eye.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from an explanation to a single-choice causal explanation.

questions.originalPrompt: Why does it help to have some micro-organisms living in the pond?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which is one way that some micro-organisms help a pond ecosystem?

options.label: They break down waste and recycle it into nutrients.
options.feedback: Correct: decomposer micro-organisms recycle material in the pond.

options.label: They block all sunlight from entering the pond.
options.feedback: Blocking all sunlight would hinder producers rather than help the pond.

options.label: They remove all oxygen from the water.
options.feedback: Removing all oxygen would harm many pond organisms.

options.label: They make the glass bowl transparent.
options.feedback: The glass is transparent because of its material, not because of micro-organisms.

feedback.correct: Correct - some micro-organisms break down waste and recycle nutrients.
feedback.incorrect: Think about decomposition and recycling material in an ecosystem.
feedback.explanation: Useful micro-organisms can break down waste, recycle nutrients, reduce disease, or provide food for other organisms.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from free text to one mark-scheme-supported benefit with controlled distractors.

sections.title: Triangles
sections.introduction: Paul investigates the sound made by metal triangles and how the size of a triangle and the force used to hit it affect the sound.

questions.originalPrompt: What happens to the triangle for Paul to hear a sound when it is hit?
questions.adaptedPrompt: What must the triangle do to produce the sound Paul hears?

options.label: Vibrate
options.feedback: Correct: the vibrating metal makes the sound.

options.label: Become hotter
options.feedback: Heating is not required for the triangle to make a sound.

options.label: Become larger
options.feedback: The triangle does not need to change size to make a sound.

options.label: Absorb the sound
options.feedback: The triangle produces sound by vibrating; it does not need to absorb it.

feedback.correct: Correct - the triangle vibrates.
feedback.incorrect: The important movement is vibration, not simply 'moving' or 'shaking'.
feedback.explanation: Sound is produced when the metal triangle vibrates.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from free text to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Write the letters A, B, C, and D to order the sound the triangles make from highest to lowest.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Order the triangles from the highest-pitched sound to the lowest-pitched sound.

feedback.correct: Correct - C, A, B, D.
feedback.incorrect: Smaller triangles produce higher-pitched sounds; larger triangles produce lower-pitched sounds.
feedback.explanation: From highest to lowest pitch, the order is C, A, B, D.

questions.adaptationNote: Original ordering task preserved as drag-and-drop or equivalent ordered controls.

questions.originalPrompt: What scientific term is used to describe how high or low a sound is?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which scientific term describes how high or low a sound is?

options.label: Pitch
options.feedback: Correct: pitch describes how high or low a sound is.

options.label: Volume
options.feedback: Volume describes how loud or quiet a sound is.

options.label: Echo
options.feedback: An echo is a reflected sound.

options.label: Force
options.feedback: Force may affect volume, but it is not the name for how high or low a sound is.

feedback.correct: Correct - the term is pitch.
feedback.incorrect: Do not confuse pitch with volume: volume is loudness.
feedback.explanation: Pitch is the scientific term for how high or low a sound is.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a one-word response to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Complete each row of the table to show how hard the triangle was hit. Use gently, quite hard, and very hard.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Classify each set of volume readings by how hard the triangle was hit.

feedback.correct: Correct - the lowest readings are gentle and the highest are very hard.
feedback.incorrect: Compare all three sets: greater force produces a greater volume.
feedback.explanation: 12/15/14 is quite hard, 8/10/6 is gentle, and 16/19/21 is very hard.

questions.adaptationNote: Original table completion preserved as a classification grid.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why Paul repeats his test three times for each force.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why should Paul repeat the volume measurement three times for each force?

options.label: To make the results more reliable and help identify an unusual reading.
options.feedback: Correct: repeated measurements provide more evidence and allow a typical result or average to be found.

options.label: To make the test fair even if he changes the force each time.
options.feedback: Repeating improves reliability; fairness depends on controlling variables.

options.label: To make sure all three readings are exactly the same.
options.feedback: Repeated readings may differ slightly; they do not need to be identical.

options.label: To increase the force each time.
options.feedback: The force should stay at the chosen level during each set of repeats.

feedback.correct: Correct - repetition improves reliability.
feedback.incorrect: Repeating does not guarantee identical results and does not by itself make a test fair.
feedback.explanation: Repeats provide more evidence, help reveal anomalous readings, and can be used to calculate an average.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from an explanation to a best-reason single-choice item.

questions.originalPrompt: Paul hit the triangle gently three times. Explain why the volume was not the same each time.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why might the three volume readings differ even though Paul tried to hit the triangle gently each time?

options.label: It is difficult to apply exactly the same force by hand each time.
options.feedback: Correct: small differences in force change the volume.

options.label: The triangle changed into a different size after each hit.
options.feedback: The triangle's size did not change, and size is linked to pitch rather than this variation in volume.

options.label: A sound sensor always chooses a random number.
options.feedback: A sensor measures sound; variation is more reasonably explained by the hits.

options.label: He struck a different place, which must always change the volume.
options.feedback: The mark scheme requires reference to the force of the hit; position alone is insufficient.

feedback.correct: Correct - the force was unlikely to be identical on every hit.
feedback.incorrect: The explanation must refer to small differences in the force or speed of each hit.
feedback.explanation: Human-applied force varies slightly, so the sound volume also varies.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from an explanation to a single-choice cause.

sections.title: Dandelion
sections.introduction: Class 5 compare the stem lengths of 20 dandelions from short grass with 20 dandelions from long grass.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box to show the most common length of dandelion stems in long grass.
questions.adaptedPrompt: What is the most common stem-length group for dandelions in long grass?

options.label: 7-10 cm
options.feedback: Only one long-grass dandelion is in this group.

options.label: 11-14 cm
options.feedback: Six long-grass dandelions are in this group, fewer than in 15-18 cm.

options.label: 15-18 cm
options.feedback: Correct: this group has the largest frequency, 11.

options.label: 19-22 cm
options.feedback: Two long-grass dandelions are in this group.

feedback.correct: Correct - 15-18 cm is the modal group.
feedback.incorrect: Look for the largest number in the long-grass row.
feedback.explanation: The largest frequency is 11, in the 15-18 cm group.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: In the table, how many dandelions had stems of 15 cm and longer?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Using both rows of the table, how many dandelions had stems of 15 cm or longer?

feedback.correct: Correct - 13 dandelions.
feedback.incorrect: Add both 15-18 cm cells and both 19-22 cm cells.
feedback.explanation: Short grass contributes 0; long grass contributes 11 + 2, giving 13.

questions.adaptationNote: Original numeric response preserved with exact numeric validation.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box in each row to show whether each prediction is supported by the evidence.
questions.adaptedPrompt: For each prediction, decide whether it is supported by the results table.

items.label: Where dandelions grow makes a difference to stem length.
There will be more dandelions in the short grass than in the long grass.

feedback.correct: Correct - only the stem-length prediction is supported.
feedback.incorrect: Both places supplied 20 sampled dandelions, so the table cannot show that one place has more dandelions overall.
feedback.explanation: The distributions differ by grass length, but equal sample sizes do not support the claim about total abundance.

questions.adaptationNote: Original evidence-classification grid preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: How is the dandelion seed usually dispersed?
questions.adaptedPrompt: How is a dandelion seed like the one shown usually dispersed?

options.label: By the wind
options.feedback: Correct: the light, parachute-like seed is carried by moving air.

options.label: By attaching to animal fur
options.feedback: This seed is adapted for wind dispersal, not hooks onto fur.

options.label: By floating along streams
options.feedback: The shown seed is not adapted for water dispersal.

options.label: By the fruit exploding
options.feedback: Dandelions do not use explosive seed dispersal.

feedback.correct: Correct - dandelion seeds are carried by wind.
feedback.incorrect: Use the parachute-like shape as evidence.
feedback.explanation: The fine hairs increase air resistance so wind can carry the seed away.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from free text to single choice while retaining the seed image.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box to show which life process seed dispersal is part of.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which life process includes seed dispersal?

options.label: Pollination
options.feedback: Pollination happens before seeds form.

options.label: Nutrition
options.feedback: Nutrition is obtaining or making food, not spreading seeds.

options.label: Reproduction
options.feedback: Correct: seed production and dispersal are parts of plant reproduction.

options.label: Growth
options.feedback: Growth is an increase in size or development, not the dispersal process.

feedback.correct: Correct - seed dispersal is part of reproduction.
feedback.incorrect: Think about the life process that produces and spreads offspring.
feedback.explanation: Seeds contain the next generation, so dispersal belongs to reproduction.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved.

sections.title: Identifying solids
sections.introduction: Mia identifies four solids by mixing them with water and vinegar and by testing a mixture with a sieve.

questions.originalPrompt: What is the name of the process that has happened to solids B and C?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Solids B and C can no longer be seen after they are mixed with water, and each liquid is clear. Which process has occurred?

options.label: Dissolving
options.feedback: Correct: the solids dissolve to form solutions.

options.label: Melting
options.feedback: Melting is caused by heating a solid into a liquid; no heating is described.

options.label: Evaporating
options.feedback: Evaporation changes a liquid into a gas.

options.label: Sieving
options.feedback: Sieving separates particles by size; it is not what happened in the water.

feedback.correct: Correct - the solids dissolved.
feedback.incorrect: A clear liquid with the solid no longer visible indicates a solution has formed.
feedback.explanation: Soluble solids dissolve in water to form a solution.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a one-word response to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Describe ONE difference between solids A and D that stops solid A going through the sieve.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which difference explains why solid A stays in the sieve while solid D passes through?

options.label: Solid A has larger particles than solid D.
options.feedback: Correct: A's particles are too large for the sieve holes.

options.label: Solid A is a different colour.
options.feedback: Colour does not determine whether particles pass through sieve holes.

options.label: Solid A is more soluble in water.
options.feedback: This test is about particle size in a dry sieve, not solubility.

options.label: Every particle of solid A is heavier.
options.feedback: The evidence supports a size difference, not necessarily a mass difference.

feedback.correct: Correct - A has larger particles.
feedback.incorrect: A sieve separates by particle size.
feedback.explanation: A stays in the sieve because its pieces are larger than the holes; D has smaller pieces.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a written comparison to a causal single-choice item.

questions.originalPrompt: Which solid has a non-reversible change when mixed with vinegar? What evidence shows the change is non-reversible?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which solid undergoes a non-reversible change with vinegar, and which observation is the evidence?

options.label: Solid C - the mixture bubbles and fizzes, showing that a gas/new material is made.
options.feedback: Correct: solid C reacts with vinegar and produces gas.

options.label: Solid B - the liquid stays clear.
options.feedback: A clear solution does not show that a new material has formed.

options.label: Solid C - the solid cannot be seen because it simply dissolves.
options.feedback: The key evidence is bubbling and fizzing, not disappearance by itself.

options.label: Solid B - the solid cannot be seen in the clear liquid.
options.feedback: Dissolving alone is reversible and is not evidence of a new material.

feedback.correct: Correct - solid C bubbles and fizzes, providing evidence that gas is made.
feedback.incorrect: Choose both the correct solid and an observation showing a new material formed.
feedback.explanation: Solid C reacts with vinegar. Bubbling/fizzing is observable evidence of gas production and a non-reversible change.

questions.adaptationNote: The original selection and written evidence are combined into one paired-choice response.

questions.originalPrompt: Draw FOUR lines to match each solid to its name. Use Tables 1, 2 and 3 to help you.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Match each lettered solid to its name using the observations from all three tables.

feedback.correct: Correct - A coconut, B salt, C bicarbonate of soda, D flour.
feedback.incorrect: Use particle size, solubility, and the vinegar reaction together; partial credit is awarded for two or three correct matches.
feedback.explanation: Coconut floats and is coarse; salt dissolves without reacting; bicarbonate reacts with vinegar; fine flour makes cloudy water and passes the sieve.

questions.adaptationNote: Original matching task preserved with exact partial-credit bands from the mark scheme.

sections.title: Celery
sections.introduction: Sandeep places celery in red-coloured water and investigates whether temperature affects how quickly the water reaches the leaves.

questions.originalPrompt: Give ONE function of the leaves for the celery plant.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which is one function of the celery plant's leaves?

options.label: They take in light and make food/new material for growth.
options.feedback: Correct: leaves use light in photosynthesis to make food for growth.

options.label: They absorb most of the plant's water directly from the soil.
options.feedback: Roots, not leaves, are the main organs that absorb water from soil.

options.label: They anchor the plant firmly in the soil.
options.feedback: Roots anchor the plant.

options.label: They create energy from nothing.
options.feedback: Leaves transfer light energy during photosynthesis; they do not create energy.

feedback.correct: Correct - leaves take in light and make food/new material for growth.
feedback.incorrect: Distinguish leaf functions from root functions, and avoid saying that leaves 'make energy'.
feedback.explanation: Leaves absorb light and carry out photosynthesis, producing sugars used for growth.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a free-text function to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: The variable I will change in my investigation is ...
questions.adaptedPrompt: In an investigation using identical celery setups but different water temperatures, which variable should Sandeep change?

options.label: The temperature of the coloured water
options.feedback: Correct: temperature is the independent variable.

options.label: The time taken for the leaves to turn red
options.feedback: Time is the measured outcome, so it is the dependent variable.

options.label: The length of each celery stick
options.feedback: Celery length should be controlled so the temperature comparison is fair.

options.label: The amount of coloured water
options.feedback: The water amount should be controlled.

feedback.correct: Correct - change the temperature.
feedback.incorrect: The changed variable is the independent variable; time is what is measured.
feedback.explanation: Temperature is varied to test its effect on how quickly coloured water reaches the leaves.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from free text to a specified experimental setup with one unambiguous independent variable.

questions.originalPrompt: The equipment I will use to measure the time it takes for the red water to get to the leaves is ...
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which equipment should Sandeep use to measure how long the red water takes to reach the leaves?

options.label: A stopwatch or timer
options.feedback: Correct: a stopwatch or timer measures elapsed time.

options.label: A thermometer
options.feedback: A thermometer measures temperature, not elapsed time.

options.label: A ruler
options.feedback: A ruler measures length.

options.label: A balance
options.feedback: A balance measures mass.

feedback.correct: Correct - use a stopwatch or timer.
feedback.incorrect: Choose equipment that measures elapsed time.
feedback.explanation: A stopwatch, clock, watch, or timer can measure the time taken.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a one-word response to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: TWO variables I will keep the same to make my investigation fair are ...
questions.adaptedPrompt: Select exactly TWO variables that could be kept the same while the coloured-water temperature is changed.

options.label: Length of the celery sticks
options.feedback: This is a valid control variable.

options.label: Amount of coloured water
options.feedback: This is a valid control variable.

options.label: Size of the glasses
options.feedback: This is a valid control variable.

options.label: Amount of food colouring
options.feedback: This is a valid control variable.

options.label: Number or surface area of leaves
options.feedback: This is a valid control variable.

options.label: Amount of light
options.feedback: This is a valid control variable.

options.label: Temperature of the coloured water
options.feedback: Temperature is the variable being changed, so it cannot also be controlled.

options.label: Time taken for the leaves to turn red
options.feedback: Time is the measured outcome, not a control variable.

feedback.correct: Correct - both selected variables can be controlled.
feedback.incorrect: Select exactly two factors that should stay constant; do not select temperature or elapsed time.
feedback.explanation: Valid controls include celery length, water amount, glass size, food colouring, leaf area, and light.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from two free-text controls to an exact-two multi-select with several mark-scheme-supported combinations.

sections.title: Jack's shadow
sections.introduction: Class 3 measure Jack's shadow in the same playground position at different times on a bright sunny day.

questions.originalPrompt: Which picture shows Jack's shadow at midday? Tick ONE box.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Select the picture that shows Jack's shadow at midday.

options.label: Top-left picture: a short 0.25 m shadow to Jack's right
options.feedback: Correct: at midday the shadow is short and lies on the side away from the Sun.

options.label: Top-right picture: a short 0.25 m shadow to Jack's left
options.feedback: The length is short, but the direction is toward the Sun rather than away from it.

options.label: Bottom-left picture: a long 2 m shadow
options.feedback: The midday Sun is higher, so the shadow should be much shorter than at 9 am.

options.label: Bottom-right picture: a long 2 m shadow in another direction
options.feedback: The midday shadow should be short, not 2 m long.

feedback.correct: Correct - the top-left picture.
feedback.incorrect: At midday the Sun is higher, producing a shorter shadow on the opposite side from the Sun.
feedback.explanation: The official answer is the top-left 0.25 m shadow.

questions.adaptationNote: Original visual single-choice format preserved with explicit position labels for accessibility.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why a shadow forms on the ground when the sunlight shines on Jack.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why does Jack form a shadow on the ground when sunlight shines on him?

options.label: Jack is opaque and blocks the sunlight from reaching part of the ground.
options.feedback: Correct: the blocked light creates the shadow.

options.label: Jack bends all the sunlight around himself.
options.feedback: A shadow forms because light is blocked, not because all light bends around him.

options.label: Any solid object makes a shadow because all solids are opaque.
options.feedback: Some solids can be transparent; the explanation must identify blocked light or opacity.

options.label: The ground becomes dark by itself when Jack stands still.
options.feedback: The darkness is caused by Jack blocking the light.

feedback.correct: Correct - Jack blocks the sunlight.
feedback.incorrect: The explanation must refer to blocked light or Jack being opaque.
feedback.explanation: Light cannot pass through Jack, so the area behind him receives less light and appears as a shadow.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from an explanation to a causal single-choice item.

questions.originalPrompt: What movement in space causes Jack's shadow to change position?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which movement in space causes Jack's shadow to change position during the day?

options.label: The Earth rotates on its axis.
options.feedback: Correct: Earth's rotation changes the Sun's apparent position in the sky.

options.label: The Earth orbits the Sun once during the day.
options.feedback: Earth's yearly orbit does not cause the day-to-day movement described here.

options.label: The Sun travels around the Earth each day.
options.feedback: This is incorrect; Earth rotates on its axis.

options.label: The Moon moves around the Earth.
options.feedback: The Moon's movement does not cause Jack's daytime shadow to shift.

feedback.correct: Correct - Earth rotates on its axis.
feedback.incorrect: Do not confuse Earth's daily rotation with its yearly orbit around the Sun.
feedback.explanation: Earth's rotation makes the Sun appear to move across the sky, changing the shadow's position.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a written explanation to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box to show why the class should not do their test on a cloudy day.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why should the class avoid doing the shadow test on a cloudy day?

options.label: Jack's shadow is very dark.
options.feedback: Clouds reduce direct sunlight, so the shadow is usually less distinct, not darker.

options.label: Jack's shadow does not change position.
options.feedback: The shadow's position still depends on the light direction; the problem is visibility.

options.label: Jack's shadow is difficult to see.
options.feedback: Correct: diffuse light on a cloudy day makes the shadow faint.

options.label: Jack's shadow is very big.
options.feedback: Cloud cover affects clarity more than making the shadow very large.

feedback.correct: Correct - the shadow would be difficult to see.
feedback.incorrect: Clouds scatter and reduce direct sunlight, making shadows faint.
feedback.explanation: A clear, bright light source is needed for a distinct measurable shadow.

questions.adaptationNote: Original single-choice format preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: Write true or false under each idea about shadows.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Classify each statement about shadows as true or false.

items.statement: The colour of a car's shadow depends on the colour of the car.
The shape of the shadow depends on the shape of the object.
You can tell if Jack's eyes are shut by looking at his shadow.
Only light from the Sun causes a shadow.

feedback.correct: Correct - false, true, false, false.
feedback.incorrect: Shadow shape follows the object's outline, but shadow colour and fine details are not shown; any suitable light source can make a shadow.
feedback.explanation: The official classifications are F, T, F, F, with one mark for any three correct and two marks for all four.

questions.adaptationNote: Original true/false task preserved with official partial-credit thresholds.

sections.title: Rolling marble
sections.introduction: John and Ravinder change the height of a ramp and measure how far a marble rolls from the bottom.

questions.originalPrompt: What equipment could be used to measure the height of the ramp?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Which equipment could measure the height of the ramp?

options.label: A ruler, metre rule, or tape measure
options.feedback: Correct: these tools measure length or height.

options.label: A stopwatch
options.feedback: A stopwatch measures time.

options.label: A thermometer
options.feedback: A thermometer measures temperature.

options.label: A piece of unmarked string
options.feedback: Unmarked string alone does not provide a height measurement.

feedback.correct: Correct - use a ruler, metre rule, or tape measure.
feedback.incorrect: Choose calibrated equipment that measures length.
feedback.explanation: The ramp height is a length, so a ruler or measuring tape is appropriate.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from free text to single choice.

questions.originalPrompt: Tick ONE box in each row to show how they should do their investigation to make sure their test is fair.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Classify each variable as something that must stay the same, must be different, or makes no difference.

feedback.correct: Correct - only ramp height changes; the surface, marble size, and marble mass stay the same.
feedback.incorrect: A fair test changes the independent variable and controls other relevant variables.
feedback.explanation: All four correct earn two marks; any three correct earn one mark.

questions.adaptationNote: Original classification table preserved with official partial-credit thresholds.

questions.originalPrompt: Explain why the ramp in photograph C is too steep to get good results.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Why is the ramp in photograph C too steep to produce good rolling-distance results?

options.label: The marble may drop, bounce, or lose contact instead of rolling smoothly down the ramp.
options.feedback: Correct: a near-vertical ramp does not provide a controlled rolling path.

options.label: The marble will simply move too fast, and speed alone makes the result invalid.
options.feedback: Speed alone is insufficient; the key problem is that the marble may fall or fail to roll along the ramp.

options.label: The ramp height becomes zero.
options.feedback: The pictured ramp is very high, not zero.

options.label: The steep ramp makes the marble permanently heavier.
options.feedback: Changing ramp angle does not change the marble's mass.

feedback.correct: Correct - the marble may drop or bounce instead of rolling smoothly.
feedback.incorrect: The explanation must go beyond saying it is fast and describe the loss of a controlled rolling path.
feedback.explanation: A very steep ramp can make the marble fall, bounce, or stop contacting the ramp, reducing measurement quality.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from an explanation to a best-explanation single-choice item.

questions.originalPrompt: Draw a cross on the graph to show the distance the marble would roll if the ramp was 0 cm high.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Select the coordinate where the point should be plotted when the ramp height is 0 cm.

feedback.correct: Correct - plot the origin, (0, 0).
feedback.incorrect: If the ramp has zero height, the model predicts zero rolling distance from the ramp.
feedback.explanation: The required point is the graph origin: height 0 cm and distance 0 cm.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from freehand plotting to a snap-to-grid coordinate selection that still tests graph interpretation.

sections.title: Candles
sections.introduction: Justine observes changes when candles burn and investigates how candle height and width affect burning time.

questions.originalPrompt: Complete the table to show if each observation is evidence of a reversible or non-reversible change.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Classify each candle observation as evidence of a reversible or non-reversible change.

feedback.correct: Correct - melting wax is reversible; smoke is evidence of a non-reversible change.
feedback.incorrect: Both rows must be correct for the mark.
feedback.explanation: Wax can solidify again, while smoke indicates new substances are produced during burning.

questions.adaptationNote: Original classification table preserved.

questions.originalPrompt: Describe the relationship between the height of the candle and the time it takes the candle to burn down to 1 cm.
questions.adaptedPrompt: Complete the relationship: The _____ the candle, the _____ it takes to burn down to 1 cm.

feedback.correct: Correct - the taller the candle, the longer it takes.
feedback.incorrect: Both variables must be compared generally, not just one specific candle.
feedback.explanation: For candles of the same width, increasing starting height increases the time needed to burn down to 1 cm.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from a written relationship to a two-slot sentence completion.

questions.originalPrompt: How many minutes did it take candle C to burn down to 4 cm?
questions.adaptedPrompt: Read the graph: how many minutes did candle C take to burn down to a height of 4 cm?

feedback.correct: Correct - the graph reading is about 23 minutes.
feedback.incorrect: Trace horizontally from 4 cm to candle C, then vertically to the time axis. Values from 21 to 26 minutes are accepted.
feedback.explanation: The expected reading is 23 minutes; the official tolerance is 21-26 minutes inclusive.

questions.adaptationNote: Original numeric graph-reading response preserved with the official accepted range.

questions.originalPrompt: Draw a line on the graph to show how quickly the new, thinner candle will burn down to 1 cm.
questions.adaptedPrompt: The new candle is thinner than candle C but starts at the same 10 cm height. Which graph line best predicts how it will burn down to 1 cm?

options.label: Line A
options.feedback: Correct: a thinner candle should burn down faster than candle C while starting at the same height.
options.accessibleDescription: A line that starts at 10 cm, falls continuously more steeply than candle C, and reaches 1 cm sooner.

options.label: Line B
options.feedback: This does not show the thinner candle burning down more quickly.
options.accessibleDescription: A line that follows the same path as candle C.

options.label: Line C
options.feedback: The new candle has the same starting height, so the line must begin at 10 cm.
options.accessibleDescription: A steep line that starts below 10 cm.

options.label: Line D
options.feedback: A burning candle should not deliberately increase in height.
options.accessibleDescription: A line that starts at 10 cm, rises, and then falls.

feedback.correct: Correct - Line A.
feedback.incorrect: The correct line must start at 10 cm, stay decreasing, be steeper than candle C, and reach 1 cm sooner.
feedback.explanation: The visual-choice format encodes all four official marking conditions without requiring freehand judgement.

questions.adaptationNote: Changed from freehand line drawing to selection among four graph-line alternatives.
